guides.title: Learn a skill fast and prove it: deliberate practice, projects, portfolio
guides.keywords: learn skill fast practice project portfolio proof show work case study tutorial hell certificate learning plan feedback build in public beginner no experience
guides.summary: You learn fastest by practising slightly beyond your level, building real projects and getting feedback. Then you turn the results into proof clients can see, since a portfolio of real work beats a list of courses.
principles: Learning is doing. Watching tutorials feels productive but skills grow when you build, get stuck, fix and repeat. Aim for a rule such as 30 percent input and 70 percent practice.

Deliberate practice means working on a specific weakness at the edge of your ability, with quick feedback. Researcher Anders Ericsson described this as the difference between mere repetition and improvement.
Project-based learning gives context. Pick a small real project (an automation for a make-believe or real business) and learn only what you need to finish it.
Feedback speeds everything up. Ask someone more experienced or a potential user to look at the work and tell you what is unclear.
Proof beats claims. Clients trust a short case study with a before, an after and what you did more than a certificate or a statement that you are good.
Show your work. Sharing progress, notes and results (honestly labelled, with permission) makes you visible and holds you accountable.
steps: Define the skill in one outcome ('build an automated lead follow-up in n8n') and a deadline of two to four weeks.
Break it into sub-skills and rank them. Choose the one that most limits your project.
Spend a short time learning (one tutorial or doc page), then immediately apply it to your project.
Practise in cycles: attempt, check against a good example or the docs, find the gap, repeat the weak part.
Finish the project to a usable standard. Label demos as demos and never present practice work as a client's work.
Write a one-page case study: the problem, what you built, how it works, the result or what you learned, screenshots or a short video.
Ask two people for feedback and improve it once. Then publish it where clients look (your profile, site, LinkedIn).
Start the next project that is slightly harder, and keep a list of finished projects.
say: [Learning goal] 'By Friday I will have built one working X, and I will show it to two people.'
[Asking for feedback] 'Could you look at this for five minutes and tell me what is confusing?'
[Being honest about experience] 'This is a demo project I built to show how I would approach it.'
[Case study title] 'How I would cut response time for a recruiting agency from hours to minutes (demo).'
[Sharing progress] 'This week I built X, learned Y, and next I will try Z.'
[To a client] 'Here is a short example of similar work so you can judge the quality.'
guides.example: Bisi wants to offer automations. Instead of another course, she picks one project: an auto-reply for a make-believe moving company. She learns the tool step by step as she builds, gets stuck twice and fixes it from the documentation, then records a 2 minute screen video and writes a one-page case study labelled 'demo'. She asks two friends and a community member for feedback, improves the explanation, and publishes it. A client later says the demo is what convinced them to book a call.
mistakes: Tutorial hell: after each lesson build something on your own.
Learning ten skills at once: pick one that serves a clear offer.
Never finishing: set a deadline and ship an imperfect version.
Presenting demos or practice as client results: label them honestly.
No feedback: ask someone every week.
Hiding the work: publish, even small, and keep improving.
guides.practice: Choose one small project you can finish in two weeks, write its one-sentence outcome and a three-step plan, and do the first step for 10 minutes now. Pick the person you will ask for feedback.
sources: Anders Ericsson and Robert Pool, Peak (deliberate practice).
Cal Newport, So Good They Can't Ignore You (craft and career capital).
Austin Kleon, Show Your Work (sharing process and results).
Josh Kaufman, The First 20 Hours (rapid skill acquisition).
Written from established frameworks in my own words; no pages fetched in this session.
